My favourite:

The reason xs-xl costs one and xxl+ costs more is because it takes more resources to make larger clothes.

"But xxl isn't much bigger than xl, why does it cost so much more?" because the cost of making xl is outweighed by the profit from xs.

Let me use a metaphor so you can understand this in the light of quantity vs profit: If you sell baskets of three eggs, four eggs, and five eggs, they can all be the same price because enough people spend money on the basket of three eggs to cover the cost of selling the basket of five eggs. Let's say you sell each basket for $4. You sell one basket of three eggs, one basket of four eggs, and one basket of five eggs. You have sold 12 eggs and you made $12. Perfect! This is the same as selling s, m, and l sizes for all the same price, because the material cost evens out.

If you sell a basket of three eggs and a basket of six eggs for the same price, you begin to lose money. If you sell one of each basket, including the one with six eggs, you now sell one basket of three eggs, one basket of four eggs, one basket of five eggs, and one basket of six eggs. You have now sold 18 eggs. But because you sell the six egg basket at the same price as the others, you now lose money because you only make $16. If you sell xxl clothes for the same price as s clothes, you lose money because the cost of material does not even out any more.

If you want to sell more baskets of more eggs, following this formula will ensure you can keep fair pricing within size ranges based on need, while keeping a profit margin.

Baskets of 3, 4, and 5 eggs: $4. Baskets of 6, 7 and 8 eggs: $7. This way, even if you sell one basket of three and one basket of eight, selling a total of 11 eggs, you still make $11.

The same is with clothing. Regular sizes have a set cost. Larger quantities have a set cost that is higher but fair within the notion that you are buying more than your small counterpart.

You can say it is not fair to the person buying 8 eggs that they have to pay more than the person buying 3 eggs, just as you are saying that buying plus size clothes for more money than a small size would cost is unfair, but you would be wrong. Someone buying only three eggs should not have to pay as much as someone buying eight eggs, it would be unfair. If you charged per egg, (or per inch of material used in clothing) the larger would still cost more and you would still complain.

If they did not sell more eggs, or larger clothes, you'd still be upset.

If they sold all egg baskets, even up to 12 eggs for still only $4, or if they sold plus sized clothes for small prices, they would quickly go out of business, jobs would be lost, and supply would disappear.

This is not discrimination. It is common sense. It is basic business. Supply and demand. Exchanging money for goods. If you buy more, you pay more.

Do you need to eat more eggs? Buy the more expensive basket of more eggs. Do you need larger clothes? Buy the more expensive larger clothes. It's simple.
